If you want to use a USB for installation (which I highly recommend!), I suggest using UNetbootin, it's a cross-platform Live-USB installer. Make sure there's nothing on your USB that you care about/need, then use UNetbootin to install the distro of your choice (I recommend debian-based distros, they're pretty friendly to start out with: Ubuntu, Linux Mint or Debian). After the OS has been installed on the USB you can reboot your PC and use your BIOS or UEFI to boot from the USB, where you'll be able to try out Linux before installing it.

If it's your first time doing something like this I recommend inviting over a friend who has done this before when you decide to install it on your PC. If you make errors in the configuration you may overwrite your windows filesystem or your personal files, so it's best to know what you're doing before you do it. I've never made an error during installation, but even now, after more than 15 years of using Linux, I still double check every configuration setting before clicking OK.

Alternatively there are a lot of in-depth guides on the internet, but they may off-putting, as there is a slight chance of large walls of text with lots of Linux jargon you may be unfamiliar with. The best way to learn is practice. Practicing in a sandbox (a VM like VirtualBox for example) will allow you to be confident with what you're doing before you actually do it on your hard-drive. (note that programs will run slower in a VM and from a Live-USB than in an actual installation!)

If you're afraid you may mess something up, the best advice is: make a backup of everything you care about, OR install linux on an empty drive! (that last one is a bit hard on a laptop, but it's easy to install a new drive on a desktop)
